why_this_tool: Schemas, indexes, partitions and query plans are all expressed and inspected in SQL itself, so practising it directly against a local Postgres is the only way to see what each design choice does.
alternatives: MySQL and SQLite speak close SQL dialects but have fewer index types and weaker partitioning; DuckDB runs analytic SQL in-process with no server; ORM layers such as Prisma or Drizzle ORM generate the SQL for you and hide the plans; migration tools such as Alembic or Flyway version the schema changes but do not design them.

setup.do: Install PostgreSQL 18 on your laptop with a package installer or a container, start the server and connect with psql.
setup.done_when: A psql prompt is open and a query for the server version returns a version 18 string.

setup.why: Every later step runs SQL against a real server you fully control. A local instance lets you break things without touching anyone's production.

setup.do: Create a practice database and a dedicated schema named shop inside it, and set your search path to that schema.
setup.done_when: Listing schemas in psql shows shop, and a new unqualified table is created in shop rather than public.
setup.why: Keeping practice objects in their own schema mirrors how real deployments separate applications and makes cleanup a single drop.

setup.do: Generate sample data with the generate_series table function: about one million orders spread over two years, plus customers and products tables.
setup.done_when: A row count on the orders table returns roughly one million rows.
setup.why: Index and plan behaviour only becomes visible at volume. Set-returning functions in the FROM clause build realistic data without any external file.

steps.do: Run a first set of queries that join orders to customers and products, filter with WHERE, and aggregate with GROUP BY and HAVING.
steps.done_when: A query returns revenue per customer per month and you can explain which join type each table uses.
steps.why: This is the first run: it confirms the data is usable and refreshes how FROM, joins and grouping compose before you start tuning anything.

steps.do: Create a new version of the customers and orders tables whose primary keys are identity columns, and try inserting an explicit key value.
steps.done_when: Inserts without a key get sequential ids, and an explicit id is rejected on the generated always table.
steps.why: Identity columns are the standard way to get surrogate keys in Postgres, and the always versus by default choice decides whether application code can override them.

steps.do: Add not null, check, unique, primary key and foreign key constraints to the tables, then run inserts and deletes that violate each one.
steps.done_when: Each bad statement fails with an error naming the constraint, and deleting a referenced customer behaves as your chosen on delete action says.
steps.why: Constraints are where schema design encodes business rules. Seeing each violation message teaches you what the database will and will not protect you from.

steps.do: Add a generated column to orders that computes the total from quantity and unit price, then try to update it directly.
steps.done_when: The total is filled in automatically on insert and a direct update of that column is rejected.
steps.why: Generated columns keep derived values consistent without triggers or application code, and they have rules about what they may reference that you should meet first-hand.

steps.do: Create one index of each main type on suitable columns: B-tree on order date, hash on an equality-only key, GIN on a JSON or array column, and BRIN on an append-ordered timestamp.
steps.done_when: Listing the table's indexes in psql shows four access methods with visibly different sizes.
steps.why: Each index type supports different operators and has a different size and write cost. Building them side by side makes the trade-offs concrete.

steps.do: Create two multicolumn B-tree indexes on customer and order date in opposite column orders, and query with a filter on only one column at a time.
steps.done_when: You can state which of the two indexes serves a customer-only filter and which serves a date-only filter, and why.
steps.why: Column order decides which queries an index can serve efficiently. The leading column rule is the most common indexing mistake in the field.

steps.do: Run EXPLAIN and then EXPLAIN ANALYZE with buffers on the queries from the previous steps, and read the plan tree from the innermost node outward.
steps.done_when: For one query you can point to the node that takes the most time and say whether it used a sequential, index or bitmap scan.
steps.why: The plan is the only reliable evidence of what a query costs. Reading scan types, join methods, estimated versus actual rows and timing is the core diagnostic skill.

steps.do: Query the planner statistics views for the orders table, load a skewed batch of rows, then run ANALYZE and compare the row estimates before and after.
steps.done_when: The estimated row count in the plan for the skewed value moves close to the actual count after ANALYZE.

steps.why: Bad plans usually come from stale or missing statistics rather than missing indexes. Seeing estimates move after ANALYZE shows what the planner is really working from.

steps.do: Write the same question, customers with no orders in the last ninety days, three ways using NOT EXISTS, NOT IN and an outer join, save each plan output to a file and compare them.
steps.done_when: Three saved plan files exist, the three queries return the same rows on null-free data, and you can name the cheapest form.
steps.why: Saving and comparing plans for equivalent queries is how you prove a rewrite is faster rather than guessing. The subquery forms also differ in how they treat nulls.

steps.do: Create a range-partitioned copy of orders with one partition per month, load the data, attach a new partition, detach an old one, and check the plan of a one-month query.
steps.done_when: The plan for a single-month query scans only one partition, and the detached month remains as a standalone table.
steps.why: Partitioning is the main tool for large time-series tables: it makes retention a metadata operation and lets the planner skip partitions that cannot match.

steps.do: Load a second set of tables with deliberately cryptic names into a separate schema, then query the system catalog schema to list its tables, columns and foreign keys and write a glossary mapping each to a business concept.
steps.done_when: You have a one-page glossary naming each table's business meaning and its relationships, built only from catalog queries.
steps.why: On a customer site the schema is often undocumented, and the catalogs plus foreign key constraints are the most trustworthy map of how entities relate. Doing this read-only keeps production safe.

steps.do: Configure a production-like layout: one schema per application owned by a dedicated role, create privilege revoked from the public schema, a read-only role with usage on the schema, and an explicit search path for each role.
steps.done_when: Connected as the read-only role, selects on the application schema succeed while a create table or an insert is refused.
steps.why: This is how a shared production database is kept safe: ownership, privileges and search path decide who can see and change what. A read-only role is what you should ask for when querying a customer's system.
